description: Music Years 1-2 width tiers — ACARA v9. All strands are capability strands; width axis is task_contexts throughout.
subject: Music

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single musical context that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For Y1-2, minimum is typically one activity type in one context.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope across the most common elaboration cases — a range of activity types (song, chant, instrumental, body percussion) in class settings. Reflects sound standard practice.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding new musical contexts, genres, purposes or cultural settings. First Nations contexts included where elaborations indicate them. Wider adds context, not difficulty.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data to ground typical_width and identify wider directions. E02 descriptor is entirely First Nations-focused; its content belongs in wider for adjacent descriptors and is the primary framing for E02 itself.

AC9AMU2C01.minimum_width: Select and combine at least two elements of music (e.g. tempo and dynamics) when composing or improvising a simple piece; practise it for informal performance.
AC9AMU2C01.typical_width: Select and combine elements of music across multiple composition and performance contexts — e.g. composing body percussion accompaniments, improvising melodies with drone, writing lyrics for a chant/rap with rhythmic patterns, using voice and instruments; use signs/symbols or recordings to document work; practise a repertoire of songs using elements such as tempo, dynamics and articulation for expressive effect.
wider: Use accessible digital technologies (recording apps, digital instruments) to capture compositions in progress, listen back and make deliberate decisions about elements of music
Compose and perform music that deliberately contrasts two or more elements (e.g. a fast/loud section contrasting with a slow/quiet section) and describe the expressive effect
Write lyrics for a chant/rap and develop rhythmic patterns to perform them — combining unison and multi-part sections with body percussion or classroom instruments
Compose music for a specific cultural purpose or occasion (e.g. a welcome song or a celebration chant) drawing on examples from diverse cultural contexts including First Nations Australian music
elaborations: contributing to decisions about how to interpret the elements of music, such as tempo, dynamics and/or articulation when performing songs, chants, rhymes or instrumental music
improvising and making decisions about how to combine sounds to create compositions; for example, combining pitch and rhythm patterns, improvising melodies and drone accompaniments
using voices and body percussion to create music that features contrasting examples of elements of music, such as sound/silence, fast/slow, long/short, high/low, loud/soft
improvising patterns of body movement, such as clapping or stamping, to create accompaniments for songs
practising a repertoire of songs, chants and rhymes focusing on using elements of music such as tempo, dynamics or articulation to create expressive effects
using signs and symbols to notate or document patterns or soundscapes and/or using an available device to record work in progress
practising music using accessible technologies; for example, using recordings to make decisions about dynamics or tempo
writing lyrics for a chant/rap and improvising to develop rhythmic patterns they can use to perform the lyrics

AC9AMU2D01.minimum_width: Demonstrate listening skills for one specific purpose (e.g. matching pitch or staying in tempo); attempt to replicate or vary a simple musical idea heard.
AC9AMU2D01.typical_width: Develop listening skills and skills for singing and playing across a range of activity types — e.g. echo clapping, call-and-response singing, pitch-matching games, singing in a group with blended dynamics; explore and improvise with a range of sound sources (voice, classroom instruments, found objects, digital instruments); practise techniques for singing songs and playing classroom instruments.
wider: Use digital tools (digital tuner, recording apps) to develop pitch awareness and self-monitor technique — listen back and adjust
Explore sounds from found and environmental objects as instruments — investigate how elements like dynamics, articulation and tone colour can be varied across unconventional sound sources
Participate in musical games from diverse cultural traditions that develop pulse, beat, rhythm and pitch awareness
Develop blending and ensemble listening skills by performing in a group and asking questions such as 'How do I know if my part is at the right volume?' and 'How does the group sound together?'
elaborations: experimenting with their speaking and singing voices/vocalisation to create a range of expressive effects
playing music games or taking part in skill-development activities to develop skills for listening, composing and performing
improvising on pitch and rhythm patterns to develop skills relevant to different elements of music; for example, echo clapping, calling and response singing
participating in singing games/activities that involve pitch awareness or matching pitch
developing listening skills for specific purposes, such as listening to count-ins, to become confident about tempo
exploring and improvising ways to create and vary sounds using a range of sound sources, such as voice, classroom instruments, found/environmental objects or digital instruments
developing understanding of what matching pitch means; for example, by using a digital tuner
practising techniques for singing songs and playing classroom instruments

AC9AMU2E01.minimum_width: Listen to music from one context or culture different from their own; share one observation about where, why or how people experience that music.
AC9AMU2E01.typical_width: Explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and other contexts experience music — e.g. listening to music from diverse contexts and identifying instruments and purposes; exploring ways people in their local community make and experience music; identifying opportunities to engage with music as composer, performer or audience in daily life; discussing music preferences with peers and family.
wider: Compile a playlist combining favourite music across different generations in a family or community group — discuss what different pieces mean to the people who love them
Investigate how music is used in screen-based products (games, cartoons, e-books) — ask 'How is the music telling me what to feel?' and 'Who made this music and why?'
Explore how being a musician takes many forms (singer, songwriter, composer, sound engineer, digital producer, audience member) — map the musicians and music experiences in the school community
Compare how music is experienced in different physical and virtual settings — live performance spaces, public spaces, streaming, ceremonies
elaborations: listening to and talking about music that features instruments and/or voices from diverse contexts and cultures, and sharing observations about the music
exploring ways that people in their local community are making and experiencing music
identifying opportunities for engaging with music in their daily life by being a composer, performer or audience
discussing where, how and why they and their peers or family members experience music, and their music preferences
practising active listening skills; for example, moving with the beat and clapping rhythmic ideas

AC9AMU2E02.minimum_width: Listen to one example of music composed or performed by First Nations Australians; identify at least one instrument or voice heard and one context in which this music is experienced.
AC9AMU2E02.typical_width: Explore diverse music styles represented in music composed and performed by First Nations Australians — e.g. via mainstream media, local festivals, choirs, orchestras, ceremonies; ask questions about instruments, voices, cultural messages and connections to Country/Place; explore how elements of music are used in screen-based or theatrical works that communicate First Nations Australian cultural knowledge.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian music communicates messages about Country/Place — use Viewpoints questions to explore how texture, melody, tempo and dynamics carry meaning
Access First Nations Australian music through multiple platforms (streaming services, live performance, school or community ceremonies) and compare how context shapes the listening experience
Explore animations or cartoons that retell traditional First Nations Australian stories — analyse how music is used to represent characters, mood and narrative tension
elaborations: identifying where and how they can experience music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians, such as via mainstream music platforms, music for ceremonies, or state and national events
exploring the diverse music styles represented in music composed and performed by First Nations Australians
exploring how the elements of music are used to create specific effects in screen-based or theatrical works that communicate First Nations Australian cultural knowledge

AC9AMU2P01.minimum_width: Sing or play a piece of music they have learnt or composed for an audience of peers; follow at least one agreed performance decision (e.g. agreed tempo or use of singing voice).
AC9AMU2P01.typical_width: Sing and play music in informal settings — performing songs, chants/raps and instrumental music; follow agreed performance decisions about sound, tempo and staging; introduce performances by sharing information about the music; listen respectfully during others' performances and contribute to post-performance discussions.
wider: Introduce a performance using a projected slide sharing information about the title, composer and context — practise how to present music to an audience, not just perform it
Make decisions about performance staging (standing vs sitting, curved vs straight rows) and justify the choice in terms of how it affects the performance and audience experience
Perform music for an audience beyond the classroom (e.g. another class, a school assembly) and reflect on how the audience and setting changed the performance
Perform music composed for a specific cultural context (e.g. a welcome or celebration song) and discuss what responsibilities performers have when performing culturally significant music
elaborations: singing songs, performing chants/raps or playing instrumental music they have learnt or composed for an audience of peers and teachers
following agreed decisions about how the music should sound; for example, using singing voice rather than speaking voice
making decisions about how/where to sit/stand in a performance space
introducing a performance by writing text for a slide that shares information about the music with the audience
listening intentionally and respectfully during performances
contributing to post-performance discussions
